Pseudo-bulk generation strategies for phenotype-guided single-cell benchmarking

Source: vignettes/pseudo_bulk_generation.qmd

Shared notation

Let

Xsc=(xgc)∈ℕG×C X^{\mathrm{sc}} = (x_{gc}) \in \mathbb{N}^{G \times C}

be the single-cell count matrix, with genes g=1,…,Gg=1,\ldots,G and cells c=1,…,Cc=1,\ldots,C.

Each cell has metadata

b(c)∈{1,…,B} b(c) \in \{1,\ldots,B\}

for barcode / organoid ID, and

yb(c)∈{0,1} y_{b(c)} \in \{0,1\}

for organoid-level phenotype, with y=1y=1 denoting successful differentiation and y=0y=0 denoting failed differentiation / neuroectodermal output.

A pseudo-bulk sample ii is generated by selecting a set of cells

𝒞i⊆{1,…,C} \mathcal{C}_i \subseteq \{1,\ldots,C\}

and aggregating their expression:

Ygiraw=∑c∈𝒞iscxgc, Y_{gi}^{\mathrm{raw}} = \sum_{c \in \mathcal{C}_i} s_c x_{gc},

where scs_c is an optional cell-level scaling factor, often sc=1s_c=1.

The normalized pseudo-bulk profile can then be written as

Ygi=Norm(Ygiraw), Y_{gi} = \mathrm{Norm}\left(Y_{gi}^{\mathrm{raw}}\right),

for example library-size normalization, TPM/CPM, DESeq2 size-factor normalization, or log transformation.

For cell-type-aware simulations, let zc∈{1,…,K}z_c \in \{1,\ldots,K\} be the cell type or state label, and let

πi=(πi1,…,πiK),∑k=1Kπik=1, \pi_i = (\pi_{i1},\ldots,\pi_{iK}), \qquad \sum_{k=1}^K \pi_{ik}=1,

be the target composition of pseudo-bulk sample ii.

Condensed comparison of pseudo-bulk generation strategies

Strategy Core idea Sampling / generation equation What is controlled? What is realistic? Main limitation Recommended use for organoid phenotype benchmarking
1. Direct organoid-barcode aggregation Treat each organoid barcode as one bulk sample. This is the closest pseudo-bulk analogue to an experimentally sequenced organoid bulk RNA-seq sample. For organoid bb: Ygbraw=∑c:b(c)=bxgcY_{gb}^{\mathrm{raw}}=\sum_{c:b(c)=b}x_{gc} Then normalize: Ygb=log⁡2(1+106Ygbraw∑gYgbraw)Y_{gb}=\log_2\left(1+\frac{10^6Y_{gb}^{\mathrm{raw}}}{\sum_gY_{gb}^{\mathrm{raw}}}\right) or use DESeq2 size factors. Real organoid-level biological heterogeneity; barcode-specific cell composition; phenotype labels yby_b. Highest realism if each barcode corresponds to a true biological organoid. Preserves natural co-variation among cell states within organoids. Limited number of bulk samples: e.g. only 8 organoids gives poor statistical power for the 8 phenotype-guided algorithms. Use as the primary benchmark if enough organoids exist. With only 8 organoids, use it as a realism anchor and complement it with bootstrap simulations.
2. Phenotype-stratified bootstrap pseudo-bulk Build many pseudo-bulk samples by resampling cells from organoids with the same phenotype. Similar to the scPP simulation logic, where phenotype-positive and phenotype-negative cells are sampled separately to create balanced pseudo-bulk cohorts. For pseudo-bulk sample ii with phenotype yiy_i: 𝒞i∼Sample{c:yb(c)=yi},|𝒞i|=Ni\mathcal{C}_i \sim \mathrm{Sample}\{c:y_{b(c)}=y_i\}, \quad |\mathcal{C}_i|=N_iYgiraw=1Ni∑c∈𝒞ixgcY_{gi}^{\mathrm{raw}}=\frac{1}{N_i}\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}_i}x_{gc} or sum first, then normalize. Number of pseudo-bulk samples; number of cells per pseudo-bulk; class balance; phenotype-specific signal strength. Retains empirical single-cell distributions and dropout patterns. Resampled pseudo-bulk samples are not independent biological replicates if drawn from the same few organoids. Can inflate apparent benchmark power. Best practical option when bulk RNA-seq is missing. Generate, for example, 50–100 pseudo-bulk samples per phenotype, but report that biological independence is limited.
3. Organoid-preserving bootstrap Resample within each barcode, then aggregate. This preserves organoid identity while creating technical pseudo-replicates. For organoid bb, replicate rr: 𝒞br∼Sample{c:b(c)=b},|𝒞br|=Nbr\mathcal{C}_{br}\sim \mathrm{Sample}\{c:b(c)=b\},\quad |\mathcal{C}_{br}|=N_{br}Ygbrraw=∑c∈𝒞brxgcY_{gbr}^{\mathrm{raw}}=\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}_{br}}x_{gc}ybr=yby_{br}=y_b Technical variability within organoids; sequencing-depth variation; cell sampling noise. Preserves barcode-specific transcriptional and compositional structure. Does not create new biological organoids; replicates are nested within barcode. Good for stress-testing algorithms while avoiding total mixing across barcodes. Use mixed-effects evaluation: pseudo-bulk replicates nested within organoid.
4. Composition-controlled Dirichlet convolution Draw target cell-state proportions from a Dirichlet distribution, then linearly mix empirical cell-type or state references. This mirrors the HADACA3-style convolution benchmark. Draw composition: πi∼Dirichlet(α)\pi_i \sim \mathrm{Dirichlet}(\alpha) Define cell-state reference means: μgk=1|Ck|∑c:zc=kxgc\mu_{gk}=\frac{1}{|C_k|}\sum_{c:z_c=k}x_{gc} Generate: Ygi=∑k=1Kμgkπik+εgiY_{gi}=\sum_{k=1}^K \mu_{gk}\pi_{ik}+\varepsilon_{gi} Cell-state proportions; rare-cell scenarios; missing or extra cell types; controlled noise. Very interpretable; known ground-truth proportions. Reference-mean convolution can be too smooth and underestimates single-cell sampling noise unless noise is added. Useful to isolate whether algorithms recover phenotype-associated states when the phenotype is encoded through known changes in πi\pi_i.
5. Empirical cell sampling from target proportions Draw proportions πi\pi_i, then sample actual cells from each cell type/state according to πi\pi_i, rather than mixing mean references. Draw: πi∼Dirichlet(α)\pi_i \sim \mathrm{Dirichlet}(\alpha) Sample counts: (Ni1,…,NiK)∼Multinomial(Ni,πi)(N_{i1},\ldots,N_{iK})\sim \mathrm{Multinomial}(N_i,\pi_i) Then: Ygiraw=∑k=1K∑c∈𝒞ikxgcY_{gi}^{\mathrm{raw}}=\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}_{ik}}x_{gc} Proportions, total number of cells, phenotype-composition coupling, rare states. Preserves empirical dropout, overdispersion, and cell-to-cell heterogeneity better than reference-mean convolution. Still assumes sampled cells can be recombined freely; may break organoid-level dependencies. Strong default for in silico benchmarking of phenotype-guided algorithms when no real bulk exists.
6. SimBu scenario-based pseudo-bulk Use predefined pseudo-bulk scenarios from SimBu. These aggregate scRNA-seq profiles under controlled cell-type fractions and optional mRNA-bias scaling. Generic form: Ygiraw=∑c∈𝒞iscxgcY_{gi}^{\mathrm{raw}}=\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}_i}s_cx_{gc} with 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_i selected according to a scenario: even, random, mirror_db, weighted, pure, or custom. Scenario-specific cell-type fractions; number of cells; number of samples; mRNA-content bias; whitelist / blacklist cell types. Practical, standardized, reproducible; can mimic compositional shifts and mRNA bias. Primarily designed for deconvolution benchmarking; phenotype labels must be added by the user. Use custom or weighted to impose success/failure-associated organoid compositions. Use mirror_db to mimic your observed organoid composition.
7. Mean pseudo-bulk with dropout correction / small epsilon Aggregate cells and stabilize zeros using a small offset before log-normalization. Similar to simple pseudo-bulk pipelines using Seurat::AggregateExpression followed by DESeq2-like normalization. Aggregate: Ygiraw=∑c∈𝒞ixgcY_{gi}^{\mathrm{raw}}=\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}_i}x_{gc} Stabilize: Ỹgi=log⁡2(Ygiraw+ϵ)\tilde{Y}_{gi}=\log_2(Y_{gi}^{\mathrm{raw}}+\epsilon) or normalize then add ϵ\epsilon. Dropout sensitivity; zero handling; library-size normalization. Simple and robust for sparse scRNA-seq. Returns essentially mean/sum expression profiles; does not model covariance or GRN structure explicitly. Use as a baseline pseudo-bulk generator. Good first-pass choice before complex generative models.
8. Gaussian latent-factor / GGM-based simulation Infer a Gaussian or latent Gaussian model from single cells, then generate pseudo-bulk by summing simulated cells. Useful when modeling gene-gene covariance or GRN-like precision matrices. For state kk: zc∣zc=k∼𝒩(μk,Σk),Θk=Σk−1z_c\mid z_c=k\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_k,\Sigma_k), \qquad \Theta_k=\Sigma_k^{-1} Generate cells: xc=zcorxc=exp⁡(zc)x_c=z_c \quad \text{or} \quad x_c=\exp(z_c) Aggregate: Yi=∑c∈𝒞ixcY_i=\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}_i}x_c Gene-gene covariance; sparse precision matrix; latent programs; phenotype-specific GRN perturbations. Can simulate coordinated gene programs rather than independent genes. If xcx_c is log-normal, ∑cxc\sum_c x_c is not log-normal. Parameters inferred at single-cell level may not transfer cleanly to bulk. Use for mechanistic stress tests, not as the only benchmark. Compare against empirical aggregation to avoid over-interpreting simulated GRNs.
9. scDesign2-like copula / marginal-dependence simulation Model gene-wise marginals with count distributions and capture dependence using copulas. Gene marginals: Xgc∼Fg(θg)X_{gc}\sim F_g(\theta_g) Dependence: Ugc=Fg(Xgc),(U1c,…,UGc)∼CρU_{gc}=F_g(X_{gc}),\qquad (U_{1c},\ldots,U_{Gc})\sim C_\rho Aggregate simulated cells: Ygiraw=∑c∈𝒞iXgcsimY_{gi}^{\mathrm{raw}}=\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}_i}X_{gc}^{\mathrm{sim}} Gene-wise count distribution; gene-gene dependency; overdispersion; zero inflation. More realistic than independent gene simulation. High-dimensional copula fitting is difficult; dependency estimates can be unstable for sparse scRNA-seq. Use to test whether algorithms are robust to realistic gene-gene dependence without imposing a mechanistic GRN.
10. Splatter / gllvm-style gene-level simulation Simulate genes using statistical count models without explicit GRNs. Typical negative-binomial form: Xgc∼NB(μgc,ϕg)X_{gc}\sim \mathrm{NB}(\mu_{gc},\phi_g) with batch, group, library-size, and dropout effects. Aggregate simulated cells: Ygiraw=∑c∈𝒞iXgcY_{gi}^{\mathrm{raw}}=\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}_i}X_{gc} Library size; dropout; group effects; batch effects; gene-level overdispersion. Good for technical noise stress tests. Does not model regulatory network structure; phenotype signal must be imposed manually. Useful negative-control simulator: ask whether algorithms falsely detect phenotype-associated cells when only technical effects differ.
11. scMultiSim / GRN + cell-cell interaction simulation Generate single-cell profiles from explicit TF-based GRNs, cell-cell interactions, trajectories, batch effects, and technical noise. Schematic form: hc=fGRN(uc,tc,CCIc,batchc)h_c = f_{\mathrm{GRN}}(u_c, t_c, \mathrm{CCI}_c, \mathrm{batch}_c)Xgc∼CountModel(hgc)X_{gc}\sim \mathrm{CountModel}(h_{gc})Ygiraw=∑c∈𝒞iXgcY_{gi}^{\mathrm{raw}}=\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}_i}X_{gc} GRNs, TF modules, trajectories, cell-cell interactions, technical noise, batch effects. Mechanistically richer than pure count simulation. More parameters; simulated mechanisms may not match organoid biology. Useful to test whether phenotype-guided methods recover known causal programs or are merely detecting composition shifts.
12. ODE / mechanistic differentiation simulator Simulate developmental trajectories mechanistically, then sample cells from success/failure attractors and aggregate. Regulatory dynamics: dzc(t)dt=f(zc(t),θ,uc)+ξc(t)\frac{dz_c(t)}{dt}=f(z_c(t),\theta,u_c)+\xi_c(t) Observed counts: Xgc∼ObsModel(zgc(tc))X_{gc}\sim \mathrm{ObsModel}(z_{gc}(t_c)) Bulk: Yi=∑c∈𝒞iXcY_i=\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}_i}X_c Differentiation dynamics; bifurcation; fate success/failure; time; perturbations. Best aligned with gastruloid differentiation biology if the model is credible. Requires strong mechanistic assumptions and parameter calibration. Use for hypothesis-driven simulations after empirical pseudo-bulk benchmarks are established.
13. DANST-style pseudo-domain alignment Generate pseudo-bulk or pseudo-spots from scRNA-seq, then align pseudo and real domains through adversarial training. Originally designed for pseudo-ST to real-ST alignment, but the idea transfers to pseudo-bulk vs real-like bulk alignment. Pseudo profile: Yipseudo=∑c∈𝒞ixcY_i^{\mathrm{pseudo}}=\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}_i}x_c Feature embedding: vi=Fθ(Yi)v_i=F_\theta(Y_i) Adversarial objective: minF,PmaxDℒpred(P(F(Ypseudo)),π)−λℒdomain(D(F(Y)))\min_{F,P}\max_D \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pred}}(P(F(Y^{\mathrm{pseudo}})),\pi) - \lambda\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{domain}}(D(F(Y))) Domain shift between simulated pseudo-bulk and target bulk-like data. Learns representations less sensitive to platform or simulation artifacts. Requires target-domain data or realistic unlabeled bulk-like profiles; more complex than direct aggregation. Use when synthetic pseudo-bulk distributions differ strongly from real bulk expectations, or when combining multiple data sources.

SimBu scenarios: compact design guide

SimBu scenario Composition rule Equation / sampling intuition Use in your organoid benchmark
even All cell types have equal fractions. πik=1/K+δik\pi_{ik}=1/K+\delta_{ik} Baseline control where phenotype should not be driven by composition unless expression programs differ.
random Random fractions over all available cell types. πi∼UniformSimplex(K)\pi_i \sim \mathrm{UniformSimplex}(K) Stress-test algorithms under broad compositional variability.
mirror_db Simulated fractions mirror the observed cell-type composition in the source scRNA-seq dataset. πi≈π̂observed\pi_i \approx \hat{\pi}^{\mathrm{observed}} Good realism baseline for your 8 organoids if you want pseudo-bulk samples to resemble the observed atlas.
weighted One selected cell type is over-represented at a specified fraction. πik⋆=w,∑k≠k⋆πik=1−w\pi_{ik^\star}=w,\qquad \sum_{k\neq k^\star}\pi_{ik}=1-w Encode success/failure by over-representing trunk-like or neuroectodermal states.
pure Only one cell type is present. πik⋆=1,πik=0(k≠k⋆)\pi_{ik^\star}=1,\qquad \pi_{ik}=0 \; (k\neq k^\star) Positive control: algorithms should easily detect phenotype-linked marker programs.
custom User supplies the full composition matrix. Π=[π11⋯π1K⋮⋮πn1⋯πnK]\Pi = \begin{bmatrix} \pi_{11} & \cdots & \pi_{1K}\\ \vdots & & \vdots\\ \pi_{n1} & \cdots & \pi_{nK} \end{bmatrix} Best choice for gastruloids: explicitly define success/failure composition designs and replicate them across pseudo-bulk samples.

Suggested benchmark design for 8 barcoded organoids

Tip

For your specific setting — approximately 20,000 single cells from 8 barcoded organoids, with four successful and four failed differentiation outcomes — avoid relying on a single pseudo-bulk design.

A robust benchmark could use three nested levels:

  1. Observed organoid pseudo-bulk

    Yb=∑c:b(c)=bxc Y_b=\sum_{c:b(c)=b}x_c

    This gives 88 realistic pseudo-bulk samples.

  2. Organoid-preserving bootstraps

    Ybrboot=∑c∈𝒞brxc,𝒞br⊆{c:b(c)=b} Y_{br}^{\mathrm{boot}}=\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}_{br}}x_c, \qquad \mathcal{C}_{br}\subseteq\{c:b(c)=b\}

    This gives technical replicates while preserving barcode structure.

  3. Phenotype-stratified or custom-composition simulations

    Yi=∑k=1K∑c∈𝒞ikxc,(Ni1,…,NiK)∼Multinomial(Ni,πi) Y_i=\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}_{ik}}x_c, \qquad (N_{i1},\ldots,N_{iK})\sim\mathrm{Multinomial}(N_i,\pi_i)

    This creates controlled success/failure pseudo-bulk cohorts with known ground truth.

Main statistical caveat

If single-cell expression vectors are independent and Gaussian,

xc∼𝒩(μ,Σ), x_c\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma),

then aggregation is simple:

Yi=∑c=1Nixc∼𝒩(Niμ,NiΣ). Y_i=\sum_{c=1}^{N_i}x_c \sim \mathcal{N}(N_i\mu,N_i\Sigma).

But if cells share organoid-level programs,

Cov(xc,xc′)=C(c≠c′), \mathrm{Cov}(x_c,x_{c'})=C \quad (c\neq c'),

then

Var(Yi)=NiΣ+Ni(Ni−1)C. \mathrm{Var}(Y_i) = N_i\Sigma + N_i(N_i-1)C.

The Ni(Ni−1)CN_i(N_i-1)C term means that shared biological programs can dominate pseudo-bulk variance. Therefore, naïve aggregation can overstate biological signal if many bootstraps reuse the same organoids.

For log-normal single-cell models,

xc=exp⁡(zc),zc∼𝒩(μ,Σ), x_c=\exp(z_c),\qquad z_c\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma),

the sum

Yi=∑cxc Y_i=\sum_c x_c

is not exactly log-normal. Moment-matching or Gaussian CLT approximations may be used, but the sparse precision matrix inferred at the single-cell level is generally not preserved after aggregation.
